verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster, 'alumoth labben'. A psalm of David.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster, to be set to the tune called Alumoth Labben: a psalm of David.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the headnote, the musical direction the Hebrew counts as verse 1, which is why the KJV numbers it 9:0 and every following verse differs by one. The performance note לַמְנַצֵּחַ names the leader, 'the one who excels' or 'the choirmaster' (from נצח), who coordinates the temple musicians. The KJV 'Muth-labben' splits the second word into עַל־מוּת לַבֵּן, 'upon the death of the son/Laban'. The Masoretic text pointed it as עַלְמוּת לַבֵּן, a single term, and nobody is sure what it means. The classical commentators give at least five readings: 'on the death of Laban' (Dunash, taken as an enemy of David), a tune or instrument (Menahem, linking עֲלָמוֹת, Ps 46:1 'for maidens', that is, high-pitched voices or harps), a Levite named Ben (1 Chr 15:18), Goliath as 'the man between the two armies', or Nabal reversed. Do not play any of them as settled: treat it as a musical direction whose meaning was already lost to the commentators. The point for the actor is that this is a psalm with a performance tradition attached.

philological_notes.note: 'To the choirmaster' or 'to the one who excels'. The same root gives נֶצַח 'perpetuity/victory' in 9:7, so a hearer of the title already meets the psalm's key word.
Unexplained tune title. Rashi on Psalm 9:1 lists readings (the death of Absalom, Nabal, a tune, the Amalek of the end of days) and says he rejects the first two; Ibn Ezra insists על מות is two words.

verses.translation_literal: I will give thanks, YHWH, with all my heart; I will recount all your wonders.
verses.translation_dramatic: With all my heart, I will give thanks to you, O LORD. I will tell it, every wonder of yours, and leave none out.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm opens in the first person singular and with two cohortatives, 'I will thank, I will tell': the singer commits himself in advance. אוֹדֶה is not the polite English 'praise'; it is public acknowledgment, to say out loud what someone did for you, and it is often done at the temple in front of others. 'With all my heart' (בְּכָל־לִבִּי) uses the Hebrew heart as the seat of thought and will, not of feeling alone. The KJV 'praise' and 'shew forth' soften two verbs of speaking: אֲסַפְּרָה is 'count out, recount', from the root that gives 'scribe' and 'number', and is the same sound as the 'telling' of a ledger. The 'wonders' (נִפְלְאוֹתֶיךָ) are rescues, not miracles in the modern sense. Play this as a man pledging himself in front of a crowd.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of ידה, 'to give thanks, to confess'. It means public acknowledgment of what God has done, which is why 'confess' (YLT) is close. Radak sees it as the thanksgiving of David and Israel for Goliath's death.
'I will recount, number off'. The verb counts items one after another, so 'all your wonders' means an enumeration, not a vague boast. Radak: one wonder prompts the telling of the earlier ones.

verses.translation_literal: I will rejoice and I will exult in you; I will make music to your name, Most High.
verses.translation_dramatic: I will be glad, I will leap for joy, and all my joy will be in you. I will sing to your name, O Most High, and make music of it.
verses.directors_commentary: Two verbs of joy in a row: שָׂמַח is gladness, עָלַץ is the louder, bodily kind, to exult or leap, so the line gets bigger as it goes. The preposition matters: the joy is בְּךָ, 'in you', not 'because of what you did'; Malbim reads this as joy in God himself, not in the rescue. The last verb אֲזַמְּרָה is 'I will play and sing', the root behind the word מִזְמוֹר, 'psalm', so the singer is saying 'I will psalm your name'. KJV 'O thou most High' keeps the old second-person 'thou' and a capital H that the Hebrew does not have; עֶלְיוֹן is an old title for the high god, used here as a name of YHWH. Cast the line with the voice rising to the last word.

philological_notes.note: 'To exult, to rejoice with the body'; rare, and stronger than שמח. The pair is a standard doublet; Metzudat Zion says the doubling is just repetition.
'Most High'. Title of God, from 'to go up'; the same title was applied to the highest god of Canaan, here claimed for YHWH alone. Radak: 'you are lifted above all'.

token_glosses.gloss: I will sing and play to

verses.translation_literal: In the turning of my enemies backward, they stumble and they perish from before your face.
verses.translation_dramatic: I watched my enemies turn their backs, and the line broke. They stumbled over their own feet, and they were gone, undone before your face.
verses.directors_commentary: The verse is one sentence with a hinge: 'when my enemies turn back' is the moment, and 'they stumble and perish' is what follows from it. Play the turn as a rout, a front rank wheeling and running, with the stumbling in the next breath. The cause is given in the last word, 'from before your face': the enemies do not simply lose, they fall away in the presence of God, as a face-to-face encounter they cannot stand. The KJV 'at thy presence' and the ASV keep this; the BBE 'before you' also does. The KJV 'they shall fall' turns a stumbling (כשל, to trip, to give way at the knee) into a fall and a prediction; the Hebrew verb is a plain 'stumble' set beside 'perish', with no future marker. 'Backward' (אחור) is the posture of defeat: an army that turns its back has stopped fighting and started running. Radak and Meiri read the scene as the Philistine army fleeing when Goliath died (1 Sam 17:51); Ibn Ezra reads it of the oppressor's people left without a king.

philological_notes.note: The infinitive with ב: 'in the turning of', 'when they turn'. The same root names turning back in retreat and, elsewhere, turning back in repentance; here it is the first meaning, the backward turn of a beaten army, made plain by אָחוֹר 'backward'.
'From before your face'. The preposition מן with פָּנִים marks the cause of the perishing: it is the divine presence that undoes them. English 'at thy presence' softens a face into an abstraction.

verses.translation_literal: For you have done my judgment and my cause; you have sat on a throne, judging righteousness.
verses.translation_dramatic: For you took up my case and you ruled on it. You sat down upon the throne, judge of what is right, and the whole matter was settled.
verses.directors_commentary: The speaker is a litigant, and the verse is a verdict. 'Judgment and cause' (משפטי ודיני) is a paired legal phrase, a doubling for emphasis; Rashi says the two words in such pairs carry no distinction, and cites Job 16:19 ('my witness and my testifier'). The singer says: my lawsuit was heard and you ruled for me. The throne is not a symbol; in the ancient Near East the king sat in judgment, and to 'sit on a throne' is to open court. The verbs are perfects, stated as done: 'you have done', 'you have sat'. The KJV 'thou satest' keeps the past tense, though in archaic dress; the ASV 'sittest' turns it into a present habit, which the Hebrew form does not give. 'Judging righteousness' (שופט צדק) is bare: the judge does not merely rule fairly, he judges in the sphere of what is right. Radak reads the verdict as the stone that struck Goliath's forehead, a God-led duel, and Meiri adds that Goliath had insulted the armies of Israel; if the psalm is David's, the 'case' is the challenge of the giant.

philological_notes.note: A legal doublet: 'my judgment and my cause'. The second word, דין, is the case itself, and the first the decision. Rashi reads the doubling as emphasis with no distinction between the words.
'You have sat on a throne': the ל stands where English expects ב ('in', 'on'). Radak and Metzudat Zion both take it so and compare Lev 26:7. To sit is to take the judge's seat.

verses.translation_literal: You have rebuked nations; you have destroyed the wicked; their name you have wiped out for ever and ever.
verses.translation_dramatic: You spoke, and nations broke at your word. You destroyed the wicked one. You wiped out their name from the world for ever and ever.
verses.directors_commentary: Three perfect verbs in a row, each with its own object, like three blows. גָּעַר is not a quiet scolding: it is the shout with which God drives back the sea or the locust, a rebuke that ends in destruction, and the Hebrew uses it without the preposition בְּ, which Ibn Ezra and Radak read as pure destruction (compare Mal 2:3). BBE's 'said sharp words' is too mild, and the KJV 'rebuked' is accurate but has a prim sound in English. Note the singular 'wicked' (רָשָׁע) after the plural 'nations': the nations are the crowd and the wicked one is their leader, which Radak, Meiri and the Targum name as Goliath, and Rashi as Amalek. 'Heathen' in the KJV is an archaic rendering of גּוֹיִם that adds a religious judgment the word does not carry; it just means 'nations, peoples'. מָחִיתָ is 'wiped out' as one wipes a slate, and the same verb wipes a name from a scroll in Exodus 17:14. In an ancient world where a name was a person's survival, this is the worst sentence. Speak it flat, without relish.

philological_notes.note: 'You rebuked', a shout that does damage, here without בְּ. Radak and Ibn Ezra compare Mal 2:3 and Ps 68:31 and read it as destroying.
'You wiped out', as a name is erased from a record. Rashi ties this to Exodus 17:14, the decree against Amalek.
'For ever and ever', literally 'for the age and continuing'. Radak notes that עד implies a longer span than עולם, and the pointing of וָעֶד changes at the verse end.

verses.translation_literal: The enemy: finished are the ruins for ever, and cities you have plucked up; their memory has perished, they.
verses.translation_dramatic: As for the enemy: his ruins are finished, finished for ever. The cities you tore up by the root are gone, and even the memory of them is gone, theirs and no one else's.
verses.directors_commentary: This is among the hardest verses in the Psalter, and the translations disagree because the Hebrew is clipped. The opening הָאוֹיֵב has the definite article, which Radak and Meiri read as the article of address, as in 'O congregation' in Numbers 15:15 and 'O generation' in Jeremiah 2:31; hence KJV and Webster 'O thou enemy'. Others take 'the enemy' as the subject of 'have come to an end', so the ASV reads 'the enemy are come to an end'. The word חֳרָבוֹת is 'ruins, wastes', and the KJV 'destructions' is a stretch: it means the heaps left after a city is razed, which is why Radak, Ibn Ezra and Malbim read it as the enemy's own ruins, the ruins he made, which have come to an end. נָתַשְׁתָּ 'you have plucked up' is a farmer's verb, to pull a plant out by the roots, and Metzudat Zion pairs it with the prophetic 'to uproot and tear down' of Jeremiah 1:10. The verse ends with a bare, emphatic הֵמָּה, 'they', which the KJV turns into 'with them'; Radak thinks it may be doubled for emphasis, or a question: are these the same cities? Play it as a eulogy delivered to the victim's face.

philological_notes.note: 'O enemy' or 'the enemy'. The article is read as a vocative by Radak and Meiri (compare Num 15:15, Jer 2:31); Ibn Ezra agrees ('and you, the enemy').
'Ruins, wastes'. Ibn Ezra reports a variant pointing with patach and prefers the reading with the hataf-qamets; Rashi reads the word as 'ruin' and compares Ezekiel 35:9.
'You plucked up', to tear out by the roots; Metzudat Zion links it with לנתוש ולנתוץ in Jeremiah 1:10.

token_glosses.gloss: they have come to an end

verses.translation_literal: And YHWH sits for ever; he has established his throne for judgment.
verses.translation_dramatic: But the LORD sits for ever. The throne is his, and he has set it in place for judgment.
verses.directors_commentary: The 'And' that opens the line is a hinge: everything before was about the dead and the forgotten, and now the subject turns, in contrast, to the one who does not go. The verb יֵשֵׁב is simply 'sits, remains, dwells', and the two meanings belong together, because a king who sits is a king who rules. Radak reads it as 'remains' (the ones before will perish, and you will stand, quoting Psalm 102), and the KJV 'shall endure' and ASV 'sitteth as king' each take one half. 'Established' (כּוֹנֵן) is the verb used for founding a city or fixing a date, and the word comes from the root of 'firm'; so God has fixed his throne in place for the purpose of judging, not for show. Rashi observes the full spelling 'his throne' (כִּסְאוֹ) against Exodus 17:16, 'the hand upon the throne of the LORD', a short form: the name and the throne are complete only once Amalek is erased. Deliver this line as calm after storm.

philological_notes.note: 'Sits, remains'. The seat of a king and his permanence are one idea. Radak: 'those perish; YHWH remains' (Ps 102:27); and Ps 29:10, 'YHWH sat at the flood'.
'He has established, made firm'. The pointing is a polel perfect of כון; the sense is a throne fixed in place for a purpose.

verses.translation_literal: And he, he will judge the world with righteousness; he will govern the peoples with uprightness.
verses.translation_dramatic: And he himself will judge the whole world in righteousness. He will rule the peoples, and all of it will be straight.
verses.directors_commentary: The two halves of the line are a parallelism: 'judge' (שָׁפַט) and 'govern, plead the case of' (דִין), 'world' (תֵּבֵל) and 'peoples' (אֻמִּים), 'righteousness' and 'uprightness'. The Hebrew begins with וְהוּא, 'and he' with an emphatic pronoun, 'he himself', and that emphasis is lost in the KJV, which also adds 'shall minister' for the second verb; there is no ministering in the Hebrew, just 'he will judge'. תֵּבֵל is the inhabited, fertile world, the land that people live on (Radak: 'the inhabited lands'), a poetic word used almost only in verse. מֵישָׁרִים is literally 'straightnesses', a plural of abstraction, like the straight road: no bending, no bribe. Rashi, a different reading, says God judged the nations by mercy until the end, and then in judgment. The line is a promise to hear in a public square, for every foreign nation listening.

philological_notes.note: 'The inhabited world', a poetic word. Radak: 'the lands where people live'.
'Straightness, uprightness', in the plural of abstraction; the opposite of crooked judgment.

verses.translation_literal: And may YHWH be a refuge for the crushed, a refuge for times in trouble.
verses.translation_dramatic: And may the LORD be a high tower for the crushed, a high tower in the times when trouble closes in.
verses.directors_commentary: The verb is a jussive, וִיהִי, 'let him be, may he be', where the KJV 'also will be' states a fact and misses the prayer. The image is physical: מִשְׂגָּב is a height too high to storm, a fortress on a rock, the word the ASV and BBE render 'high tower' and the KJV flattens to 'refuge'. Anyone who has seen a hill town in Judah knows what the crushed need: a place that attackers cannot reach. The word דַּךְ is 'crushed, pounded', the same root as 'dust' and 'contrite' (דכא); it is a person physically ground down, as grain is in a mortar (Metzudat Zion: 'broken and pounded'), which is stronger than the KJV's 'oppressed'. 'Times in trouble' (לְעִתּוֹת בַּצָּרָה) is a compressed Hebrew phrase, and Meiri takes the prefix as redundant. Say the repeated word 'high tower' slowly, as if climbing it.

philological_notes.note: 'A height, a secure stronghold'. The root means 'to be high, inaccessible'; the image is a fortress on a rock. Radak compares a strong tower (מגדל עז).
'Crushed, broken'. Rashi connects the word with דַּכָּא in Ps 90:3 and sees Israel as the crushed party; Metzudat Zion glosses 'broken and pounded'.

verses.translation_literal: And may they trust in you, those who know your name; for you have not forsaken those who seek you, YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let them trust in you, all who know your name. For you have never left those who come looking for you, O LORD.
verses.directors_commentary: This is a wish, said over a congregation. The verb וְיִבְטְחוּ follows directly on the jussive 'may the LORD be a refuge' of the verse before (וִיהִי), and the form is the same short imperfect with a vav: 'and may they trust', 'let them trust'. The KJV and ASV 'will put their trust' make it a forecast and lose the prayer. Radak says it is only right that they should trust (דין הוא שיבטחו), which is the sense of the volitive; Ibn Ezra reads that when they see the LORD as a refuge for the crushed, they will be secure. 'Those who know your name' is not those who have heard it: to know the name is to have met the one who bears it. Radak glosses it as 'Israel today, who have seen'; take this as his own reading of the occasion. The reason clause is a statement of experience in the perfect: 'you have not forsaken', and the verb 'seek' (דרש) is the same one that opens 9:13 for God's 'seeking out' of blood. Seekers are sought. The name YHWH is held to the very last word, after the reason, as if the speaker could not say it until the claim was safely made.

philological_notes.note: Short imperfect with vav after the jussive וִיהִי of 9:10: 'and may they trust'. The verb means to rest one's weight on someone, hence trust that holds. A wish, not a prediction.
'Those who know your name': knowing here is relationship and experience, not information. Radak specifies it of Israel in the day of the psalm, who had seen what the name did.

verses.translation_literal: Make music to YHWH, who sits in Zion; declare among the peoples his deeds.
verses.translation_dramatic: Sing to the LORD, who sits enthroned in Zion! Tell the nations what he has done, and let them hear it from you.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm turns here from 'I' to 'you', a plural imperative, and the congregation is called to join in. The same verb for singing as in verse 3 is used, זַמְּרוּ, 'play and sing'. 'Dwelleth in Zion' in the KJV loses a pun: יֹשֵׁב is the same verb as in verse 8, 'he sits (enthroned)', so the LORD who sits for ever on his throne is the one who sits in Zion, and the throne is a real place. The commentators raise a historical problem: if David wrote this, Zion was still held by the Jebusites, so Radak and Meiri read it as prophecy. Do not smooth that over; it is a live tension. 'Deeds' (עֲלִילוֹתָיו) is a stronger word than KJV 'doings': עֲלִילָה is a notable act, a feat or a piece of conduct that has consequences, and it can be sinister when used of people (Ps 14:1). Here it is mission: the nations are the audience, not just the enemies.

philological_notes.note: 'Who sits in Zion', the same verb as the throne in v. 8. Radak and Meiri note Zion was still Jebusite in David's time and take the phrase as prophetic.
'His deeds, his acts', actions with consequences. Metzudat Zion glosses it 'his works'.

verses.translation_literal: For the seeker of bloods, he has remembered them; he has not forgotten the cry of the humble.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the one who calls blood to account has not lost it from his mind. He remembers every one, and he has never forgotten the cry of the humble.
verses.directors_commentary: Blood here is plural, 'bloods' (דמים): spilled lives, and the violence that spilled them. God is the one who 'seeks' them, the verb of a legal inquest, of an avenger who comes asking where the dead are. The KJV 'when he maketh inquisition' turns a title into a time clause and puts a 'when' where the Hebrew has the ongoing identity of God, 'the seeker of bloods'. The word at the end carries a textual note. The consonants written in the text are עניים, 'afflicted ones'; the tradition reads the word as ענוים, 'humble ones', and the printed vowels follow the reading. The KJV 'humble' follows the reading; the ASV 'poor' and YLT 'afflicted' lean to the written form. Radak says it is written with yod and read with vav, adding that the humble are in effect the poor and the weak, since the poor are for the most part humble. Meiri says much the same. In 9:19 the pair is reversed, so this does not repeat there. The cry (צעקה) is the scream of the wronged, the one the law says God hears (Exod 22:22 in the usual reading, not cited by the commentaries here). Radak reads the bloods as those the Philistines shed in Israel.

philological_notes.note: 'The seeker of bloods': the verb means to inquire into, to seek out, and in the legal sense to demand an accounting. 'Bloods' in the plural names blood shed in violence. Radak reads them as those shed by the Philistines in Israel.

Ketiv/Qere: written עניים ('afflicted'), read ענוים ('humble'). The printed vowels follow the Qere. The two words overlap in meaning, as Radak and Meiri say: the poor are mostly the humble. The pair is reversed at 9:19.

verses.translation_literal: Show me favor, YHWH; see my affliction from my haters, [you who are] raising me from [the] gates of death,
verses.translation_dramatic: Be gracious to me, LORD. Look at what I am suffering at the hands of those who hate me, you who have lifted me again and again from the very gates of death.
verses.directors_commentary: The voice drops from certainty to need. After the confidence of verse 13 the singer speaks in the imperative: 'chaneni' (show me favor, from the root of 'grace'), then 're'eh' (see). Hebrew often asks God to look, because in the biblical world to see is to act. The KJV's 'consider my trouble' is a little too cool; the Hebrew has 'see my affliction', and the preposition 'min' ('from' those who hate me) means the affliction comes from them. The closing phrase, 'the gates of death', is a concrete picture. A city's gates are its entrance, so the gates of death are the threshold of the underworld, and the singer says he has stood at them. The participle 'meromemi' is present and habitual: 'you who lift me', which makes the memory a basis for the request, as Metzudat David reads it ('Have you not always lifted me from the gates of death?'). Rashi and Malbim set this in later situations, exile or Laban, and Radak in the fight with Goliath; the Psalm itself names none. Look ahead: these 'gates' answer the 'gates of the daughter of Zion' in the next verse.

philological_notes.note: 'Gates of death': the entrance to the realm of the dead, found also in Job 38:17 and Psalm 107:18. Radak: 'near to death, like the gate to the house'. It is the counterpart of the 'gates of Zion' in 9.15.
A prayer for grace, an unearned favor. Radak notes the pointing with qamets in the printed text of his day and links it to the verb in Genesis 42:21 ('when he pleaded with us').

verses.translation_literal: So that I may recount all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion; I will rejoice in your deliverance.
verses.translation_dramatic: So that I may tell it all, every praise of yours, in the gates of the daughter of Zion. There I will rejoice, for you have saved me.
verses.directors_commentary: The verse is built as a contrast with 9:14: 'the gates of death' there, 'the gates of the daughter of Zion' here. Ibn Ezra says it so, 'against the gates of death'. The speaker asks to be lifted from one gate in order to stand in the other. The city gate was the public square of an ancient town, where elders sat, cases were heard and news was told; to recount praises there is to speak before the whole community. Radak points to Deut 25:7 for the gate as the place of the elders. 'Daughter of Zion' personifies the city as a young woman, which the KJV keeps. The sentence breaks at the atnach on Zion: 'so that I may recount all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion' is one half, and 'I will rejoice in your deliverance' the other. The ASV moves the break so that 'in the gates of the daughter of Zion' attaches to the rejoicing; the KJV and YLT keep the Hebrew division. The BBE 'house' for 'gates' drops the civic image. 'Deliverance' (ישועה) is the word the KJV renders 'salvation': in the Bible it is a rescue from danger in the body and in the world, first of all, before any later theological sense. Radak says תהלתיך is written as a plural without the vav, 'praises', and that 'all' means all the praises for the rescues the speaker has himself lived through; Meiri says the same.

philological_notes.note: 'In the gates of the daughter of Zion': gates as the place of public assembly and judgment, set against the 'gates of death' of the verse before. Ibn Ezra reads the pairing explicitly.
Written without the plural vav, 'your praise', but read as a plural, 'your praises'. Radak says the defective form stands for the plural.
Cohortative: 'let me rejoice', 'I will rejoice'. Malbim distinguishes גיל from simple joy: a joy over something newly happened.

verses.translation_literal: Nations have sunk in [a] pit [which] they made; in [the] net, this [one] which they hid, their foot has been caught.
verses.translation_dramatic: The nations have gone down into the pit they dug themselves. The net they hid in the grass has closed on their own feet.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the first praise the singer promises: a trap that closes on the trapper. Hebrew has two hunting images side by side. A 'shachat' is a pit, dug and covered to catch game; a 'resheth' is a net spread on the ground. Malbim notes that hunters used both together, and both turn on their makers. The verbs are matched, too: they 'made' it, they 'hid' it, and it is their own foot that is caught. The irony is the point, and the Psalm says it as moral order, not luck. The KJV's 'heathen' is a fine word for 'goyim', but the Hebrew only says 'nations'. Its 'are sunk down' is correct: 'tave'u' is the verb used for drowning or sinking in mud. Note the little word 'zu', 'this one': the net is pointed at, as if the singer could see it. Radak takes the nations as the Philistines, Meiri the same; the verse names no one. In the dramatic reading keep the pace slow and the images close to the ground.

philological_notes.note: A relative or demonstrative: 'which' or 'this'. Radak: 'zu' is like 'asher' (which), and compares Isaiah 42:24; Ibn Ezra takes it as 'eleh' (these).
A pit, a hunter's trap; the word is related to the root for 'destroy', which gives the sound play on ruin (shachat) and the sinking of the nations.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH has made himself known; [a] judgment he has done; in [the] work of his palms [the] wicked [is] snared. Higgaion. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD has made himself known. He has judged, and the judgment is plain: the wicked man is caught in the work of his own hands. Be still, and think on it.
verses.directors_commentary: Here the Psalm states its lesson. 'Nodah' is a Niphal form: YHWH has made himself known, reflexively, by acting. The KJV's 'is known by the judgment which he executeth' turns it into a passive and ties the knowledge to the act, which is fair, but the Hebrew has three short clauses, each a flat statement: he is known, he has done justice, the wicked is snared. The last is the sharpest. 'Ka-paw' is 'his palms', the cupped hands that make things; the trap is a tool he made, and he is caught in it. Radak links this to Goliath, killed with his own sword (1 Samuel 17:51); the Psalm does not say so. The verse ends with two musical or liturgical markers. 'Higgaion' comes from a root that means to murmur, to mutter, to meditate, and is perhaps a call to reflect or a soft instrumental passage; its sense is uncertain. 'Selah' has no agreed meaning; it is commonly taken as a pause or lift. The KJV transliterates both, as does this text. For performers: this is a place for silence.

philological_notes.note: From hagah, to mutter, murmur, meditate. Rashi: 'let this be recited'; Radak: 'this deliverance is for us a theme and a thanksgiving'; Metzudat Zion: thought, as in 'the meditation of my heart' (Psalm 19). Its exact musical sense is unknown.
A participle meaning snared or caught in a trap (moqesh). Radak and Meiri derive it from the same root as 'moqeshim', snares; Ibn Ezra and Radak's alternative read a root nqsh as in Psalm 38:13.

verses.translation_literal: The wicked will return to Sheol, all [the] nations [who are] forgetters of God.
verses.translation_dramatic: The wicked will go back down to Sheol, every nation that has forgotten God.
verses.directors_commentary: The verse is short and cold, and should be played that way. 'Yashuvu' is 'will return', not 'will be turned', as the KJV has it; the verb is the common one for going back, and Radak sets it beside Genesis 3:19, 'to dust you shall return'. Sheol is the underworld of the Hebrew Bible, the shadowy place of the dead, not a place of fire; the KJV's 'hell' reads a later Christian picture of punishment into it and was inherited by Webster. The ending 'lish'olah' has a directional he on the end, 'toward Sheol', which the rabbis noticed (Rashi cites Yevamot 13b and gives the reading 'to the lowest level of Sheol'); this is a tradition added to the text, not its plain sense. Metzudat David notes that 'return' pictures someone coming back to a house made ready for them. The second half is a title: 'shekhekhei Elohim', 'forgetters of God'. This is the other side of verse 13, where God does not forget the humble: here the nations forget him. The Hebrew sets the two verbs 'sh-kh-ch' at either end of the Psalm's moral scheme.

philological_notes.note: Sheol with a directional ending (-ah): 'to Sheol'. The rabbis (Rashi, citing Yevamot 13b) read the extra letters as the lowest level.
'Forgetters', the construct plural of the adjective shakheach. The same root as 'he has not forgotten' in 9.13 and 'will be forgotten' in 9.19, so the three verses play on it.

verses.translation_literal: For not to perpetuity will the needy one be forgotten; the hope of [the] afflicted ones will not be lost for ever.
verses.translation_dramatic: No. The needy will not be forgotten for ever. The hope of the afflicted will not be lost. Not for ever, not for good.
verses.directors_commentary:
This verse is the hinge between the nations' fall (v. 18) and the plea of vv. 20-21, and it answers the question the whole psalm has circled: who is remembered? Say it as a promise made against the evidence. The speaker looks at people who have been ground down and says, flatly, that their hope is not a thing that can be thrown away.

The Hebrew has two different words for the poor. אֶבְיוֹן (evyon) is the one who has to ask, the beggar who needs what others have. עָנִי (ani) is the one pressed down, bent under another's hand. Neither is a middle-class 'poor man' of the modern sort: in a village economy, a debt or a drought, or one powerful neighbour, could turn a family into an evyon within a season, and there was no safety net but the court of the king and the gate of the elder. A promise that God will not forget them is a promise about law and power as well as comfort.

The verse works by wordplay on time: לָנֶצַח (la-netzach, 'to perpetuity') in the first line and לָעַד (la-ad, 'for ever') in the second, framing the hope between two words for 'always'. The KJV's 'shall not alway be forgotten' is a pleasant archaism, but 'alway' hides the stronger 'to perpetuity'. Its 'expectation' for תִּקְוָה (tikvah) is also faint: tikvah is hope with a cord in it (the root can mean a taut line), something held on to, which is why Rahab's scarlet cord is called a tikvah in Joshua 2:18.

There is also a textual wrinkle for the actors to be aware of. The word 'afflicted' is written one way and read another. The written text (Ketiv) has עֲנָוִים (anavim, 'the humble'), and the reading tradition (Qere) says עֲנִיִּים (aniyyim, 'the afflicted'). Radak says the two are close in sense, since the afflicted are mostly the humble. At 9:13 the pair is the reverse: written 'aniyyim, read 'anavim. Neither Hebrew form is softened by the KJV, which simply gives 'poor' (and 'needy' for evyon), flattening the difference between the two words.

philological_notes.note: 'Hope of', from tikvah. The root qvh means to wait, to stretch toward something, and gives qav 'a line, a cord'. The hope here is something stretched and held, not a mood. The KJV 'expectation' is accurate but cooler than the Hebrew.
Qere 'aniyyim, 'afflicted, bowed down'; Ketiv 'anavim, 'humble'. At 9:13 the written and read forms are the other way round. Radak: the afflicted are mostly the humble.

'Will be lost, will perish'. The earlier verses use the same verb of the wicked (9:4-7, 9:6 'their memory has perished'), so the hope of the poor is set against the lost name of the nations. The single 'not' of the first line carries over to this verb, as Radak and Metzudat David observe.

verses.translation_literal: Arise, YHWH! Let not humankind prevail; let nations be judged upon your face.
verses.translation_dramatic: Rise up, LORD! Do not let mere man win the day. Let the nations stand to be judged before your face.
verses.directors_commentary: The mood turns to command. 'Qumah' is the cry used when the ark set out in the wilderness (Numbers 10:35): 'Arise, YHWH'. It is the call that asks God to move from waiting to action, and Radak says it is only a figure, since God does not literally sit or stand. 'Enosh' is the word for a human as a frail creature, from a root of weakness (Radak points to Jeremiah 30:12; Metzudat Zion to Jeremiah 17:9, 'and he is sick'), so 'let not Enosh prevail' sets the weak against the Eternal, and the KJV 'man' loses the sting. 'Ya'oz' is 'be strong, be defiant'. The last phrase, 'al panekha', is 'upon your face'. The KJV and ASV smooth it into 'in thy sight'; Radak and Meiri take it as 'before you'; Rashi and Metzudat David read 'face' as anger ('on account of the anger'). The Hebrew keeps the physical image: the nations are to stand before the face of the judge. YLT's 'before Thy face' is closest. The KJV's 'heathen' is a loaded label; the Hebrew says only 'goyim'.

philological_notes.note: Humankind as weak and mortal. Radak derives it from 'anash', to be sick, citing Jeremiah 30:12; Metzudat Zion cites Jeremiah 17:9.
'Upon your face': Radak and Meiri read it as 'lifnekha', before you; Rashi and Metzudat David read 'face' as 'anger'.

verses.translation_literal: Set, O YHWH, fear for them; let them know, nations: human [are] they. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: Set fear in them, O LORD. Let the nations learn it at last: they are only human. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary:
The prayer turns from the poor to the proud, and the actors should hear that the request is not for slaughter but for a lesson. The goal is knowledge: יֵדְעוּ, 'let them know'. What the nations are to learn is the smallest thing: that they are אֱנוֹשׁ (enosh), mortal, breakable.

The Hebrew order is the whole point. אֱנוֹשׁ הֵמָּה, 'human [are] they': the predicate comes first, the pronoun after it, so that the word 'human' lands like a verdict and 'they' is almost an afterthought. English 'they are but men' (KJV) puts the pronoun first and adds the little word 'but', which the Hebrew does not have. Enosh is also the word for weak, mortal humanity as opposed to God (compare Jeremiah 17:9 'sick'; Radak ties it to the root of 'incurable', Jeremiah 30:12), so the line echoes verse 20, where the same word appears: 'let not enosh prevail'. The poem is built on this one word: the proud claim strength, and the prayer is that they will be called by their weak name.

The first line is a puzzle that the classical commentators argue about. The word מוֹרָה (morah) is spelled with a final ה, but most of them (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri) take it as a variant spelling of מוֹרָא (mora), 'fear', which is what the KJV's 'put them in fear' reflects. Others hear 'throwing, casting down' (Rashi, Metzudat Zion, from the verb of Exodus 15:4, 'he cast into the sea'), and Rashi also offers 'mastery, yoke'. A third reading, 'a teacher' (YLT 'a director'), is grammatically natural, since moreh is the ordinary word for a teacher; but it is a different noun and with a feminine ending it does not fit. 'Fear' is the best reading, and the actors should play it that way, but the sense of someone being 'cast down' is in the air.

Selah, the last word, is a marker of uncertain meaning: perhaps a pause, a musical lift, an instruction to the singers. The KJV keeps it as a bare transliteration, which is right. In performance, let the line end and hold the silence.

philological_notes.note: Read as a spelling of mora 'fear' (ה for א), the majority view; others give 'throwing' (from yarah, as in Exodus 15:4), 'yoke', or, as moreh, 'teacher'. The meaning 'fear' fits the plea best.
Literally 'human [are] they': the predicate 'human' first, the pronoun 'they' after it. Enosh is mortal, frail humanity, as against God. There is no verb 'to be' in the Hebrew, and no 'but'.
A term of uncertain meaning, probably a musical or liturgical marker (pause, interlude, lift of voice). Ibn Ezra glosses it 'truly'. Left untranslated.
